item.title: Explained: What are dark GPUs and how are they holding back the AI boom?
item.description: Power shortages are leaving billions of dollars' worth of AI chips unused at data centres. Here's what dark GPUs are, why they matter and how they could slow the AI boom ...
item.dc:creator: Rimjhim Singh
item.content:encoded: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has run into an unexpected problem: some of the world's most powerful computer chips are sitting idle because data centres do not have enough electricity to run them, Business Insider reported. These unused chips, known as 'dark GPUs', highlight a growing gap between the pace of investment in AI infrastructure and the availability of power to support it. Business Insider reported last week that Amazon was buying billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia AI systems even as some of its data centres lacked the electricity needed to operate them. Internal company emails reviewed by Business Insider showed that Amazon Web Services (AWS) expected to receive about $5 billion worth of Nvidia GB300 server racks in August this year, followed by around $3 billion worth every month. Some of the equipment was being stored in warehouses until the required power infrastructure became available. What are dark GPUs? A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialised computer chip designed to handle several calculations at the same time. Unlike a central processing unit (CPU), which handles a wide range of general computing tasks, GPUs can process large amounts of data simultaneously. This makes them particularly useful for AI applications, including training large language models, generating images and running AI-powered services. Companies such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google buy thousands of these chips and install them in data centres, where they work together in server racks to provide computing capacity. Dark GPUs are not a separate category of chips. The term refers to GPUs that have been purchased but remain unused because they cannot be switched on or fully utilised. This could be due to inadequate electricity supply, incomplete data centre infrastructure or problems with system design that prevent the hardware from being used efficiently. Why are GPUs sitting idle? The biggest reason is the shortage of electricity and the time required to build supporting infrastructure. AI data centres consume large amounts of electricity because they house thousands of powerful chips that need to operate continuously. They also require cooling systems to prevent the equipment from overheating, along with networking infrastructure to connect the servers. However, building a data centre and securing the required electricity supply can take years. Grid connections, transmission infrastructure and approvals can delay projects even after companies have purchased the hardware. As a result, chips may arrive before the facilities are ready to accommodate them. Research organisation Epoch AI estimated in December 2025 that GPUs account for about 40 per cent of the electricity used by frontier AI data centres at peak operation. Cooling, networking and other infrastructure account for much of the remaining consumption. What problems do dark GPUs create? • Billions of dollars tied up in idle equipmentGPUs are expensive, and companies often spend billions of dollars securing supplies. When these chips remain unused, the investment does not immediately generate revenue. In Amazon's case, its Early Rack Receipt programme allows it to take ownership of server racks earlier in the supply chain. While this helps the company secure scarce Nvidia hardware, it also means money is tied up before the equipment starts generating revenue. • Higher costs and financial pressureCompanies must also bear costs associated with storing, maintaining and eventually installing the equipment. They may need additional financing while waiting for data centres to become operational. • Delays in AI servicesWhen computing infrastructure is not ready, companies cannot deploy the full capacity they have purchased. This can delay the expansion of cloud computing services and the availability of computing resources for AI developers and businesses. • Pressure on the wider supply chainThe problem could extend beyond data centre operators. A Reuters report on October 5, citing Morgan Stanley, said US data centre developers faced an estimated net power shortfall of 34 per cent, or 32 gigawatts, through 2028. The brokerage warned that delays in deploying AI infrastructure could also affect demand for memory, optical and other chip components. Is the problem getting bigger? Recent developments at Amazon suggest that the infrastructure challenge is continuing even as technology companies increase their AI investments. On Thursday, Amazon reiterated its plan to spend $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, with Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Andy Jassy saying the company expected to spend even more in 2027. The company's results for the third quarter showed that its free cash flow had turned negative by $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months. Jassy, however, said Amazon had strong visibility into customer demand for AI computing capacity through 2027, 2028 and 2029. Amazon's third-quarter results showed its free cash flow turned negative, with an outflow of $42.4 billion over the trailing 12 months. The company attributed the decline primarily to higher spending on property and equipment, driven by AI investments.

item.title: Big tech's $750 billion AI bet faces strain with slowing core growth
item.description: The earnings reports and the ensuing stock selloffs expose the tensions escalating over big tech's transition to new AI-powered products, and the spending required to get there ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Julia Love and Spencer Soper The core businesses of America’s technology giants — the advertising, consumer and retail machines propping up a collective $750 billion in AI spending this year — are starting to show signs of slowing. In some cases, they’re being cannibalized by the very technology the firms are betting the house on. Earlier this week, Google owner Alphabet Inc. reported that ad sales from search and other channels — a business line that accounts for roughly half of overall revenue — grew at the slowest pace in five quarters. Yet the company maintained a capital spending outlook of as much as $205 billion for this year. Amazon.com Inc. said Thursday that growth in both its core ecommerce juggernaut and the advertising business slowed last quarter, before reiterating its plan for roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year. Microsoft Corp. and Meta Platforms Inc. similarly maintained their spending guidance, while posting results that ultimately underwhelmed investors.  The earnings reports and the ensuing stock selloffs expose the tensions escalating over big tech’s transition to new AI-powered products, and the spending required to get there. The companies have been issuing unprecedented levels of debt, selling equity, signing multibillion-dollar data center deals and taking on trillions of dollars in future obligations to pay for a worldwide build-out of AI infrastructure. All this while new products are eroding the profitability and drawing attention away from some of their legacy offerings.  Investor patience is wearing thin. Alphabet’s shares plunged by a record on Thursday, wiping out nearly $500 billion in market value. Amazon’s stock was down 7% in late trading. Meta has fallen 10% since reporting earnings last week, when it told investors that it plans to bet even more aggressively on AI while warning that the new agentic AI app Muse is proving to be incredibly computing intensive.  The market is “scratching its head — how does all this pay off?” Dan Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, said following Alphabet’s earnings.   Even Microsoft, which reported strong growth in its cloud business and kept spending in check, couldn’t avoid the fallout. The company’s shares initially surged after the firm reported that sales at Azure, the closely watched cloud computing division, grew 48% to $33.2 billion during the quarter ending in September. By the time markets closed on Thursday, the stock had erased all gains and was down 0.2%.  Amazon’s results were more nuanced. The company had shifted its annual Prime Day from the third quarter last year to the second quarter this year, which explained some of the slowdown. But analysts had already adjusted their estimates with that in mind, and results still came up short. The commerce giant’s advertising services unit saw growth of 11%, the slowest pace since Amazon first broke it out as a separate category in 2022. And the online stores business grew by just 2%, a level not seen in more than three years when people resumed pre-pandemic spending habits and online shopping cooled.  Those results overshadowed the growth of Amazon’s cloud-computing segment and stoked investors’ doubts about its aggressive investments in AI. Cloud computing was also a bright spot for Google. The cloud division’s sales more than doubled from a year earlier. Operating income more than tripled. The unit’s chief executive officer, Thomas Kurian, joined the earnings call for the first time, signaling the business’ importance to Google going forward.  But investors were more fixated on the cracks emerging within Google Search, which remains the lifeblood of the company. To stay relevant as chatbots such as ChatGPT become more popular, Google has woven more AI into the search engine, including a dedicated tab called AI Mode. But the growing popularity of that feature has hurt the profitability of Google Search. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler acknowledged on Wednesday that the firm is seeing “lower monetization” for queries with AI Mode, an admission that sent its stock falling further. Schindler said the company is working to bring more ads to AI Mode and is optimistic about the product’s trajectory. Google has struggled this year to keep up in the AI race against startups Anthropic and OpenAI. If the company can regain footing on AI model development, it will likely resume delivering the returns that investors have come to expect, said Mandeep Singh, an analyst with Bloomberg Intelligence. “With all these transitions, sometimes we get too fixated on the cash cow business,” Singh said. “Given how Cloud has been expanding margins, I feel a combination of the cloud business and search, once they are at the frontier, would take their profitability back to where they were.” It’s also common for new ad formats to launch with lower margins that gradually increase over time, Gene Munster, managing partner of Deepwater Asset Management, said of Google’s lower AI Mode monetization. The firm’s larger challenge is building agents that can make purchases on behalf of users and pocketing a cut of those transactions — a business model that many in Silicon Valley believe is within reach after the success of Meta’s Muse personal assistant.  “The old way of doing it was blue links or display advertising to influence consumer behavior,” Munster said. “The new way is how do you influence the bot.”

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / Commodities / Oil prices rise on supply concerns as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia

Oil prices rise on supply concerns as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia Brent crude futures rose 86 cents, or 0.75%, to $115.74 a barrel as of 0122 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose 72 cents, or 0.71%, to $102.72

For the month, Brent was on course to finish nearly 14% higher, while WTI was heading for a 15% jump to close above $100 for the first time since April

Reuters SINGAPORE 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 8:45 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Oil prices climbed in early trade on Friday on supply concerns after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, on track for a fourth straight monthly gain and the steepest since July. Brent crude futures rose 86 cents, or 0.75%, to $115.74 a barrel as of 0122 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose 72 cents, or 0.71%, to $102.72. For the month, Brent was on course to finish nearly 14% higher, while WTI was heading for a 15% jump to close above $100 for the first time since April. On Thursday, the Houthis said they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including its largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, the Rabigh refinery and an Aramco facility in Abqaiq, while a Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.

"Continued kinetic action around the Strait of Hormuz amidst doubts of a viable diplomatic pathway are keeping oil prices elevated in expectation of an escalation of the conflict in coming weeks," said MST Marquee Head of Energy Research Saul Kavonic. Also Read

BFSI Insight Summit 2026: 'Lower taxes may bring back foreign investors'

Oil rises after attack on Saudi Arabian refinery reignites supply concerns

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country get medical supplies, after US media reported Vance had written to Tehran's top security official to revive peace talks. Iran has received a letter from Vance but it has not responded to it yet, the country's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported, while adding that Tehran wants the US to meet its conditions and "any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable."

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit sea mines, exploded and caught fire while attempting to use an unauthorised route south of the Strait of Hormuz. Amid security concerns in the region, ExxonMobil and Chevron have cancelled plans for their executives to travel to the United Arab Emirates' biggest oil show next week, two sources familiar with the developments told Reuters.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / Cryptocurrency / Binance's possible hack triggers $3 billion freeze in crypto assets

Binance's possible hack triggers $3 billion freeze in crypto assets The market impact of the possible hacking, which could be the largest-ever crypto heist according to analytics firm Chainalysis, was felt immediately in early Asian trading on Friday

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has more than 335 million registered users globally and had about $160 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2024 annual report (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 7:25 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it had frozen $3 billion in crypto assets as it investigated a potential security breach, with stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether freezing related assets.   "Binance will cover all hacking losses," Binance co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.   The market impact of the possible hacking, which could be the largest-ever crypto heist according to analytics firm Chainalysis, was felt immediately in early Asian trading on Friday.   Bitcoin dropped about 2% to a six-week low of $77,646 and ether fell around 2% to a two-month low of $2,238.76. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down more than 8% over the past 24 hours at $694, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.

Crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. Also Read

Crypto investors must research; invest only what they can lose: Experts

BFSI Insight Summit: Crypto industry calls for greater regulatory clarity

Crypto industry leaders flag tax hurdles, seek regulatory clarity in India

Crypto boom or risk trap? Experts explain what young investors need to know

Tokenisation offers common ledger for real-world assets, says Edul Patel

Binance said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.   Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident "looked like a hack."   Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has more than 335 million registered users globally and had about $160 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2024 annual report.

BINANCE HAS SECURE ASSET FUND   Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, according to its website, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches.   "It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them, said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.   "My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size."   Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.

Binance said it was conducting security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It added user funds remained safe and that teams were reviewing the incident.   The exchange also temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution.   World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.   Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.

INCIDENT ADDS TO STRING OF CRYPTO THEFTS   Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown actor, though the exact cause had not been confirmed. Morel said the incident began around 4:30 p.m. EDT (2030 GMT) and appeared to be ongoing.   The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.

Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.   Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.   Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.   In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
